title: Google Cloud revenue more than doubles as Alphabet posts Q3 2026 blowout
subtitle: Google Cloud revenue reached $30.7 billion on 103% year-over-year growth and Alphabet's total revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion, driven by TPU system sales and enterprise AI demand that the company said accelerated from the prior quarter.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Alphabet reported third-quarter 2026 results after the close on Wednesday, October 28. Consolidated revenue rose 25% year over year to $127.6 billion — the company's 13th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. Google Cloud revenue reached $30.7 billion on 103% year-over-year growth, up from 82% last quarter, with the company specifically citing TPU system sales plus enterprise AI infrastructure and enterprise AI solutions as drivers. Google Services revenue was $96.3 billion with Search & other growing 12% — a growth rate the company said was the highest for Search queries in five years. Operating income rose 30% to produce a 31.8% operating margin, net income available to common stockholders was $26.2 billion, and diluted EPS was $2.12.

The cloud number is the result that reframes the earnings-week debate. Google Cloud grew 103% off a base of $24.8 billion, which means the quarter added more than $15 billion of annualized revenue in three months. Alphabet raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195–$205 billion in the summer, and this is the first quarter where the growth curve on the revenue side matches the shape of the spending curve. TPU systems — Google's custom AI accelerators, now sold directly to other hyperscalers and large AI labs including Anthropic — moved from a line Alphabet began recognizing last quarter to a meaningful contributor it called out explicitly. For reference, Google Cloud's backlog was $514 billion at the end of Q2.

This is the second shoe to drop in a week that opened under pressure. Four Democratic senators asked the Financial Stability Oversight Council last month to probe hyperscaler data-center financing. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the sector did not pose systemic risk but acknowledged firms had not explained the public benefit well. Nasdaq had sold off repeatedly on AI-cost concerns. Alphabet's print, combined with Microsoft's Azure growth jumping to 48% the same evening (covered separately in today's digest), gives the capex thesis its clearest defense yet: at least two of the four hyperscalers are generating AI revenue fast enough to keep pace with the balance sheets they're building. Whether Meta, which drifted into negative free cash flow last quarter, and Amazon, which reports Thursday night, can do the same is the question that remains open.

A note for learners: watch the operating-margin line, not just the revenue line. 103% cloud growth is impressive on its own, but the fact that Alphabet's overall operating margin held at 31.8% while capex ran at a $200-billion annual pace means the capital intensity has not yet broken the business model. If next quarter's cloud growth stays triple-digit and operating margin holds, the market will reprice AI infrastructure as a durable platform. If cloud growth decelerates sharply or operating margin compresses while capex climbs, that same model gets re-examined. The ratio of capex to incremental revenue is the number this cycle will be judged on, and today Alphabet's version of that ratio looked healthier than most analysts expected.
